title: Data modeling and SQL
tagline: Tables, keys, joins, and constraints: the shape of the data decides which bugs are possible.
why: Many bugs that look like application logic are really data-shape bugs: a report that double counts, a filter that silently skips rows, an orphan that crashes a nightly job. If you can read a schema and predict what a join returns, you can tell a wrong number from a wrong model in minutes. Constraints and migrations decide which bad data can ever exist and whether a deploy can freeze the database.
objectives: Read a small schema and name each table's primary key and the relationships between tables
Predict how many rows a join returns and spot when a total has been multiplied
Explain why a comparison with NULL matches nothing and fix the filter
Choose which rules belong in database constraints and which in application code
Describe an expand-and-contract migration and say which schema changes can lock a busy table

blocks.text: A relational database stores data in **tables**. Each table holds one kind of thing, each row is one instance of it, and each column is one typed attribute. A **primary key** is the column, or set of columns, whose value identifies exactly one row and never repeats.

A **foreign key** is a column that holds another table's primary key, so a row can point at its parent. In Relay, each message points at its ticket and each ticket points at its user. The database can check that every pointer leads somewhere.

blocks.title: Relay's core tables, simplified
blocks.code:
users        id PK | email UNIQUE | name | created_at
tickets      id PK | user_id FK -> users.id | status | created_at
messages     id PK | ticket_id FK -> tickets.id | role | body | created_at
orders       id PK | user_id FK -> users.id | total_cents | placed_at
refunds      id PK | order_id FK -> orders.id | ticket_id FK -> tickets.id
             | amount_cents | created_at
tags         id PK | name UNIQUE
ticket_tags  ticket_id FK -> tickets.id | tag_id FK -> tags.id
             | PK (ticket_id, tag_id)
notes: Read each FK as 'many of these belong to one of those'. Many tickets belong to one user; many messages belong to one ticket.
`refunds` has two parents. A refund belongs to an order, and records which support ticket caused it.
`ticket_tags` exists only to connect tickets and tags. Its primary key is the pair, so the same tag cannot be attached to a ticket twice.
The foreign key always sits on the 'many' side. That is where to look when you want to know who points at whom.

blocks.caption: Relationship shapes
rows: Meaning
Each row matches at most one row on the other side
One parent, any number of children
Each side can match many on the other
Where the key lives
A unique foreign key on either side
A foreign key on the child
A join table holding both keys
Relay example
A user and their notification settings
A ticket and its messages
Tickets and tags
Typical mistake
Forgetting the UNIQUE, so 'one' quietly becomes many
Storing child IDs as a list inside the parent
A comma-separated tag string that cannot be joined or checked
blocks.verdict: Name the relationship before you design or debug a table. Most row-count surprises come from treating a one-to-many as a one-to-one.

blocks.text: Natural or surrogate keys

A **natural key** is a real-world value that happens to be unique, such as an email address or an order number printed on a receipt. A **surrogate key** is a meaningless value the database generates only to identify the row. Natural keys change: customers change emails, and every foreign key holding the old value must change with them.

blocks.title: Email as the primary key
blocks.text: If `users.email` is the primary key, every ticket, order, and refund stores the email. A customer who changes address forces updates across all of them, and any table that missed the update now points at nobody. Use a surrogate `id` as the key and put a UNIQUE constraint on email.

options.name: Auto-increment integer
gain: New rows append at the end of the index
Easy to read in logs and support tickets
cost: Only the database can assign it
Reveals volume and is easy to guess
A 32-bit column runs out near 2.1 billion
options.choose: Choose this for internal tables with one database, using a 64-bit type from the start.

options.name: Random UUID
gain: Can be generated anywhere, before the insert
Safe to merge data from several sources
cost: 16 bytes in the key and in every index and foreign key
Random values scatter inserts across the index
Hard to read aloud or compare by eye
options.choose: Choose this when IDs are created outside the database, appear in public URLs, or come from several systems.

options.name: Time-ordered UUID
gain: Roughly increasing, so inserts stay near the end of the index
options.choose: Choose this when you want UUID benefits on a large, insert-heavy table, using a variant such as UUIDv7.

blocks.title: Hard-to-guess IDs are not access control
blocks.text: If a customer can open `/tickets/1043` and see another customer's ticket, switching to UUIDs only makes that harder to stumble on. The real fix is a server-side check that the ticket belongs to the caller, covered on Day 16.

blocks.q: Relay wants to record which tags apply to each ticket. A ticket can have several tags and a tag applies to many tickets. Where do the keys go?
options: A join table with a ticket ID and a tag ID per row
A `tag_id` column on the tickets table
A `ticket_id` column on the tags table
A comma-separated list of tag names on each ticket
blocks.explain: Many-to-many needs a table of pairs. A single `tag_id` on tickets allows only one tag per ticket, a `ticket_id` on tags allows only one ticket per tag, and a text list cannot be joined, indexed, or checked by a foreign key.

blocks.text: A **join** combines rows from two tables wherever a condition matches, usually a foreign key equal to a primary key. The result has one row per matching pair. Nearly every surprising number from SQL comes from forgetting that it is one row per *pair*.

blocks.caption: What each join returns
rows: Returns
Only pairs where the condition matches
Every left row, with its matches or with NULLs
Every left row paired with every right row
Left row with no match
Disappears from the result
Kept once, right-side columns NULL
Not applicable, since there is no condition
Row count
One per matching pair
One per matching pair, at least one per left row
Left count times right count
Typical bug
Customers with no orders vanish from a report
A WHERE condition on the right table turns it back into an inner join
A forgotten join condition produces it by accident
blocks.verdict: Use an inner join when unmatched rows should be excluded, and a left join when every row on the left must appear. Ask how many matches each left row can have before trusting any total.

blocks.text: How a join multiplies rows

Joining one parent to two different child tables pairs every child of the first kind with every child of the second. A user with 2 orders and 3 tickets becomes 6 rows. Any SUM or COUNT over those rows counts each order three times and each ticket twice.

blocks.title: A per-customer report that triples revenue
blocks.code:
-- ana has 2 orders (4000 and 6000 cents) and 3 tickets
SELECT u.email,
       SUM(o.total_cents) AS spent_cents,
       COUNT(t.id)        AS tickets
FROM users u
JOIN orders  o ON o.user_id = u.id
JOIN tickets t ON t.user_id = u.id
GROUP BY u.email;

 email           | spent_cents | tickets
-----------------+-------------+---------
 ana@example.com |       30000 |       6
notes: Before grouping there are 2 x 3 = 6 rows for ana. Each order appears once per ticket.
The true spend is 10,000 cents and the true ticket count is 3. Both numbers are wrong, by different factors.
Users with no tickets vanish entirely, because both joins are inner joins.
`SUM(DISTINCT o.total_cents)` is not a fix. It would also merge two different orders that happen to have the same amount.

blocks.title: A total changed after someone edited a query
blocks.text: Count the rows before grouping and compare `COUNT(*)` with `COUNT(DISTINCT o.id)`. If they differ, rows are repeated. The usual fix is to aggregate each child table separately per user, then join the small results.

**GROUP BY** collapses all rows that share the grouping key into one row per group, and aggregates such as SUM and COUNT are computed within each group. Aggregates run after the join, so they faithfully sum whatever rows the join produced, duplicates included.
NULL and three-valued logic

**NULL** means the value is missing or unknown. Comparing anything with NULL, even another NULL, gives UNKNOWN rather than true or false. A WHERE clause keeps only rows where the condition is true, so rows that evaluate to UNKNOWN silently drop out.

blocks.title: Counting tickets by assignee
blocks.code:
SELECT count(*) FROM tickets;                            -- 10,000
SELECT count(*) FROM tickets WHERE assignee_id = NULL;   -- 0
SELECT count(*) FROM tickets WHERE assignee_id IS NULL;  -- 2,500
SELECT count(*) FROM tickets WHERE assignee_id <> 7;     -- 7,100
SELECT count(assignee_id) FROM tickets;                  -- 7,500
notes: `= NULL` is never true, so it matches nothing. `IS NULL` is the test that works.
`<> 7` returns 7,100, not 9,600. The 400 tickets assigned to 7 are excluded, and so are the 2,500 unassigned ones.
`count(*)` counts rows; `count(column)` skips NULLs. Averages skip NULLs too.

blocks.title: NOT IN with a NULL inside
blocks.text: `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT ticket_id FROM refunds)` returns no rows at all if any `ticket_id` in refunds is NULL, because every comparison with that NULL is UNKNOWN. `NOT EXISTS` behaves the way people expect.

blocks.q: A report should list every user with their open tickets, if any. It uses `users LEFT JOIN tickets` with `WHERE tickets.status = 'open'`. Users with no open tickets are missing. Why?
options: The WHERE condition drops rows whose ticket columns are NULL
A left join returns only users who have tickets
The status comparison needs `IS 'open'` instead of `=`
The query needs a GROUP BY on the user
blocks.explain: The left join keeps unmatched users with NULL ticket columns, then the WHERE tests `NULL = 'open'`, which is UNKNOWN, so those rows are dropped. Moving the status condition into the join's ON clause keeps them.

blocks.prompt: An average resolution time over all tickets looks suspiciously good. Many tickets are still open and have a NULL `resolved_at`. What is the average actually measuring?
blocks.answer: Only resolved tickets, because averages skip NULLs. The slowest tickets, the ones still open, are left out entirely, so the average is biased low. Report the open count next to it, or measure age for open tickets separately.

blocks.text: **Normalization** means storing each fact once, in one place, and pointing to it from everywhere else. The normal forms are formal rules for this, and their practical summary is short: if a value can change, it should live in exactly one row.

Suppose Relay copied the customer's email into every ticket row. When the customer changes their email, old tickets keep the old one unless every copy is updated. Reports then disagree depending on which copy they read. That is the cost duplication always carries.

blocks.title: Store each fact once, or copy it where it is read

options.name: Normalized
cost: Some list pages get slower as tables grow
options.choose: Choose this by default, for any data that changes and must be correct.

options.name: Denormalized
gain: A row is self-contained for display or export
cost: Every copy must be updated on change
Copies drift apart when an update path is missed
options.choose: Choose this deliberately for read-heavy paths, or for values that should freeze in time, such as the price on a past order.

blocks.title: Some copies are facts of their own
blocks.text: An order's total at checkout should not change when the product's price changes later. Storing it on the order is a separate fact, the price paid, and not duplication. Ask whether the copy should follow the original or stay frozen.
Constraints are tests that run on every write

blocks.caption: Constraints in Relay's schema
rows: NOT NULL
A missing value
`tickets.status`
A ticket no queue picks up because its status is empty
UNIQUE
A second row with the same value
`users.email`
Two accounts for one customer after a double-click
CHECK
A row failing a condition on its own columns
`refunds.amount_cents > 0`
A negative refund that pays the store
FOREIGN KEY
A pointer to a row that does not exist
`refunds.order_id`
A refund for an order nobody can find
blocks.verdict: Put every rule that must never be broken into a constraint. The database then checks it on every write, from every code path, including scripts and the agent's tools.

blocks.title: What constraint violations look like in PostgreSQL
blocks.code:
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "users_email_key"
DETAIL:  Key (email)=(ana@example.com) already exists.

ERROR:  insert or update on table "refunds" violates foreign key constraint
        "refunds_order_id_fkey"
DETAIL:  Key (order_id)=(91822) is not present in table "orders".

ERROR:  new row for relation "refunds" violates check constraint
        "refunds_amount_cents_check"
notes: The constraint name tells you which rule fired; Postgres names them after the table and column unless you choose a name.
DETAIL shows the offending value. A foreign key error with an ID nobody recognizes often means the caller invented or mistyped it.
In Python these arrive as exceptions from the driver. An API that turns them into 500s is hiding a 409 or 422.

blocks.caption: Where to enforce a rule
rows: Runs when
Every write, from any client
Only on code paths that call it
Bypassed by
Almost nothing
Scripts, admin tools, other services, a forgotten path
Concurrent requests
Safe: two inserts cannot both pass a UNIQUE
Two requests can both pass a check and both insert
Error quality
Generic, needs translating for users
Clear, specific, and friendly
Rules it can express
Simple ones about a row or a key
Anything, including calls to other systems
blocks.verdict: Enforce invariants in the database and also check them in the application for good error messages. Keep rules that need other systems or business judgment in code.

blocks.title: Check, then insert
blocks.text: Relay's sign-up code checks that no user has an email, then inserts. Two requests a few milliseconds apart both pass the check and both insert. Only a UNIQUE constraint closes the gap; Day 10 covers this race in depth.

blocks.title: Orphaned rows
blocks.text: When a job crashes on a child whose parent is gone, look for a missing foreign key. A left join from child to parent where the parent's id is NULL lists the orphans. Clean them up, then add the constraint so the database refuses the next one.

blocks.title: Constraints catch agent mistakes
blocks.text: When the model calls `issue_refund` with an order ID it made up, a foreign key rejects the write instead of storing a refund for nothing. A CHECK rejects a negative amount. These are guardrails that do not depend on the prompt.

blocks.q: Duplicate accounts keep appearing for the same customer, differing only in letter case, such as `Ana@x.com` and `ana@x.com`. There is a UNIQUE constraint on `email`. What closes the gap?
options: A unique index on the lowercased email
A CHECK that the email contains an @
An application check before each insert
A foreign key from users to emails
blocks.explain: A UNIQUE on the raw column treats different cases as different values. A unique index on `lower(email)` makes the database compare them the same way. An application check alone still loses the race between concurrent sign-ups.

blocks.text: A **migration** is a versioned script that changes the schema, such as adding a column or an index. Migrations run in order, and a tool records which ones have run, so every environment ends up with the same schema. Alembic, common with SQLAlchemy, keeps the current version in a table of its own.

Many schema changes need a strong lock on the table. While a change waits for that lock, every new query on the table waits behind it. A change that is instant on an idle table can stall a busy one for as long as the oldest open transaction keeps running.

blocks.caption: Schema changes on a large, busy PostgreSQL table
rows: Add a nullable column
A catalog change, with a brief exclusive lock
Low, unless it waits behind a long transaction
Change a column's type
Usually rewrites the whole table and its indexes under an exclusive lock
High: reads and writes block for the whole rewrite
Add NOT NULL to a column
Scans every row to verify, under an exclusive lock
Medium to high on large tables
Create an index
Blocks writes until built, unless built concurrently
High without the concurrent option
Add a foreign key
Checks every existing row
Medium; can be added unvalidated, then validated with a lighter lock
Drop a column
A quick catalog change
Running code that still reads the column starts failing
blocks.verdict: Treat any change that rewrites or scans a large table as an operation to plan, not a routine deploy step.

blocks.title: Expand and contract: renaming `name` to `full_name` with no downtime

steps.label: Expand: add `full_name`, nullable
steps.detail: A quick change. Old code ignores the new column.
steps.fail: Run without a lock timeout, it can queue behind a long transaction and stall the table.

steps.label: Deploy code that writes both columns
steps.detail: Every new or edited user now has both values.
steps.fail: A write path that was missed leaves new rows with only the old column.

steps.label: Backfill old rows in batches
steps.detail: Copy `name` into `full_name` a few thousand rows at a time, with short transactions.
steps.fail: One giant UPDATE holds locks for its whole run and produces a burst of writes that replicas must replay.

steps.label: Deploy code that reads `full_name`
steps.detail: Reads switch only after the backfill is verified.
steps.fail: Switching early shows empty names for rows the backfill has not reached.

steps.label: Stop writing `name`
steps.detail: No running code touches the old column any more.
steps.fail: An old version still running during a rolling deploy breaks if the column vanishes too soon.

steps.label: Contract: drop `name`
steps.detail: The last step, often in a later release.
steps.fail: Dropping before every reader is gone produces errors in whatever still selects it.

blocks.title: A migration locked a table
blocks.text: In `pg_stat_activity`, look for queries with wait event type `Lock` and find what blocks them with `pg_blocking_pids`. The usual chain is an old `idle in transaction` session, then the migration, then every request. Set a short `lock_timeout` in migrations so they fail fast instead of queuing.
What an ORM hides

An **ORM**, or object-relational mapper, maps tables to classes and rows to objects, so you write Python and it writes the SQL. What it hides is when queries happen and how many. With **lazy loading**, related objects are fetched only when first accessed, one query at a time.

blocks.title: SQLAlchemy with SQL logging on, while a loop reads each ticket's messages
blocks.code:
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine SELECT tickets.id, tickets.status
FROM tickets
WHERE tickets.user_id = %(user_id_1)s
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine [generated in 0.00019s] {'user_id_1': 4410}
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine SELECT messages.id, messages.body
FROM messages
WHERE %(param_1)s = messages.ticket_id
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine [generated in 0.00012s] {'param_1': 812}
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine SELECT messages.id, messages.body
FROM messages
WHERE %(param_1)s = messages.ticket_id
INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine [cached since 0.004s ago] {'param_1': 813}
notes: One query loads the tickets, then one more query runs per ticket as the loop touches its messages. With 200 tickets that is 201 queries.
Nothing in the Python loop looks like database access. Only the SQL log shows it.
For SQLAlchemy, `echo=True` on the engine prints this. Most ORMs have a similar switch. Day 9 covers fixing this pattern.

options.name: ORM
gain: Less boilerplate for ordinary reads and writes
Schema and code stay in one language
cost: Query count and shape are hidden
Lazy loading causes many small queries
options.choose: Choose this for routine create, read, update, and delete work, with SQL logging available when you debug.

options.name: Raw SQL
gain: You see and control every query
Full use of the database's features
cost: More code to write and keep in sync with the schema
Easy to build queries unsafely by pasting strings
options.choose: Choose this for reports, bulk operations, and hot paths where the exact query matters.

blocks.title: The ORM model is not the schema
blocks.text: A model class can say a column is required while the database allows NULL, or the reverse. Data written by scripts or older code follows the database, not the class. When they disagree, believe the database and check its constraints directly.

blocks.prompt: A migration that adds a nullable column to `messages` took 0.2 seconds in staging. In production, the API stalled for four minutes while it ran. What most likely made the difference?
blocks.answer: The migration waited for its lock behind a long-running or idle-in-transaction session in production, and every query on `messages` queued behind the migration. Staging had no such session. A `lock_timeout` would have made it fail fast and retry instead.

fieldGuide.symptom: A report total doubled, or tripled, after someone added a join
causes: The new join is one-to-many, so each existing row repeats once per match
Two child tables joined to the same parent multiply each other
fieldGuide.look: The query's joins, and the row count before GROUP BY compared with the count of distinct parent IDs.
fieldGuide.confirm: `COUNT(*)` is larger than `COUNT(DISTINCT parent.id)` for the same rows.
fieldGuide.fix: Aggregate each child table separately and join the results, or filter with EXISTS instead of joining.

fieldGuide.symptom: A filter returns no rows, or fewer than expected, on a column that has NULLs
causes: `= NULL` or `<> value` comparisons evaluate to UNKNOWN for NULL rows
`NOT IN` over a list that contains a NULL
fieldGuide.look: How many rows have NULL in the filtered column.
fieldGuide.confirm: Counts with `IS NULL` account exactly for the missing rows.
fieldGuide.fix: Use `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL` explicitly, and `NOT EXISTS` instead of `NOT IN`.

fieldGuide.symptom: Every request touching one table hangs during a deploy, then recovers all at once
causes: A migration waits for a lock behind a long transaction, and new queries queue behind it
A migration rewrites the table under an exclusive lock
fieldGuide.look: `pg_stat_activity` during the stall: sessions waiting on `Lock`, and `idle in transaction` sessions with an old start time.
fieldGuide.confirm: `pg_blocking_pids` on the waiting queries leads to the migration, and from the migration to an old transaction.
fieldGuide.fix: Cancel the migration, then rerun it with a `lock_timeout`, or restructure it as expand and contract.

fieldGuide.symptom: A nightly job crashes on messages whose ticket no longer exists
causes: No foreign key, so parent rows were deleted while children remained
A cleanup script deletes parents directly
fieldGuide.look: A left join from child to parent where the parent ID is NULL.
fieldGuide.confirm: Orphans exist and the table has no foreign key on that column.
fieldGuide.fix: Decide what orphans mean, clean them up, then add the foreign key with an explicit ON DELETE rule.

fieldGuide.symptom: Two accounts exist for the same customer email
causes: Uniqueness is checked only in application code, which loses races
fieldGuide.look: Duplicate emails grouped by `lower(email)`, and their creation timestamps.
fieldGuide.confirm: Pairs created milliseconds apart, or differing only in letter case.
fieldGuide.fix: Merge the duplicates, then add a unique index on the normalized email.

fieldGuide.symptom: Inserts fail with 'integer out of range' or 'reached maximum value of sequence'
causes: A 32-bit integer primary key ran out near 2.1 billion
fieldGuide.look: The ID column's type and the sequence's current value.
fieldGuide.confirm: The sequence value is at the 32-bit maximum.
fieldGuide.fix: Move to a 64-bit ID with an expand-and-contract migration. Changing the type in place rewrites the table under a lock.

fieldGuide.symptom: A backfill made the whole database slow and replicas fell behind
causes: One UPDATE over millions of rows in a single transaction
fieldGuide.look: Running statements, their start times, and replica lag during the backfill.
fieldGuide.confirm: Slowness starts and ends with the backfill statement.
fieldGuide.fix: Backfill in small batches with short transactions. It takes longer in total but never holds the database for long.

fieldGuide.symptom: An API returns 500 when a customer submits a form twice
causes: A unique or foreign key violation is raised and not translated
The application assumes its own check already prevented duplicates
fieldGuide.look: The exception in the logs: the constraint name and the DETAIL line.
fieldGuide.confirm: A `duplicate key value violates unique constraint` error appears at the time of the 500.
fieldGuide.fix: Catch the constraint error and return a 409 or 422 with a clear message. Keep the constraint.

fieldGuide.symptom: A page that shows one list runs dozens or hundreds of queries
causes: ORM lazy loading inside a loop
fieldGuide.look: The ORM's SQL log for one request.
fieldGuide.confirm: One query for the list, then one near-identical query per item.
fieldGuide.fix: Load related rows up front with the ORM's eager loading option. Day 9 covers this pattern.

glossary.def: The column or columns whose value identifies exactly one row in a table. It must be unique and not NULL.
A column holding another table's primary key, plus a constraint that the referenced row must exist.
A generated identifier with no real-world meaning, such as an auto-increment integer or a UUID.
A real-world value that happens to be unique, such as an email or order number. It can change, which makes it a risky primary key.
A join that returns one row for each pair of rows matching the condition. Rows with no match on either side are dropped.
A join that keeps every row from the left table, filling the right side with NULLs where nothing matches.
Collapses rows sharing the same key into one row per group, so aggregates such as SUM and COUNT are computed per group.
A marker for a missing or unknown value. Comparisons with it yield UNKNOWN, which WHERE treats as not true.
Designing tables so each fact is stored once and referenced elsewhere, so an update touches one row.
Deliberately copying data into the rows that read it, to avoid joins, at the cost of keeping copies in sync.
A rule the database checks on every write, such as NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, or FOREIGN KEY, rejecting rows that break it.
A versioned script that changes the schema, applied in order and recorded so each environment runs it once.
Changing a schema with no downtime by adding the new shape, moving code and data over in steps, then removing the old shape.
Object-relational mapper: a library that maps tables to classes and rows to objects, generating SQL for you.

apply.title: Read your own data model as a set of rules
steps: Pick the place your project stores structured data, such as eval results, conversation logs, or a SQLite or Postgres database. Write down each kind of record, its unique key, and which other records it points to.
For each pointer, write what happens if the target is deleted, and whether anything stops it today.
Find one value stored in two places, such as a model name kept with each result and in the run config. Decide whether the copy should follow the original or stay frozen.
If you use SQL or an ORM, turn on SQL logging (for SQLAlchemy, `echo=True` on the engine), run one script or page, and count the queries it emits.

quiz.q: A query joins each customer to their orders and to their support tickets, then sums order totals per customer. The grand total is about three times the sum of the orders table. What is the most likely cause?
options: Orders were inserted twice by a retrying client
The join repeats each order once per ticket of the same customer
SUM counts NULL totals as zero and inflates the result
The GROUP BY is missing one of the selected columns
quiz.explain: Joining two child tables to the same parent produces one row per order-ticket pair, so each order is summed once per ticket. Duplicate inserts would also show in the orders table's own sum, which is correct here.
why: Duplicates in the table would inflate the table's own sum too, which matches the true total.
SUM skips NULLs, and adding zero cannot inflate anything.
A missing GROUP BY column causes an error in PostgreSQL, not a larger number.

artifact.code:
SELECT count(*) FROM tickets;                          -- 10,000
SELECT count(*) FROM tickets WHERE priority = 'high';  -- 1,200
SELECT count(*) FROM tickets WHERE priority <> 'high'; -- 6,300

quiz.q: Why do the last two counts not add up to 10,000?
options: The counts ran at different moments while tickets were being inserted
`count(*)` skips rows that contain any NULL value
2,500 tickets have a NULL priority, and neither comparison is true for them
Some rows say 'High' with a capital letter and match neither filter
quiz.explain: For a NULL priority, both `= 'high'` and `<> 'high'` evaluate to UNKNOWN, so those rows fall out of both counts. Case differences are tempting, but 'High' is not equal to 'high', so those rows land in the second count.
why: Concurrent inserts could explain a handful of rows, not a gap of 2,500.
`count(*)` counts every row; only `count(column)` skips NULLs.
'High' is different from 'high', so those rows satisfy `<> 'high'` and are counted.

quiz.context: Relay's web app shows tickets at `/tickets/1042`. A customer changes the number to 1043 and sees someone else's ticket.
options: Switch ticket IDs to random UUIDs so they cannot be guessed
Encrypt the ticket ID in the URL
Rate limit ticket lookups per customer
Check on the server that the ticket belongs to the caller
quiz.explain: The bug is a missing ownership check. Random UUIDs make IDs hard to guess, which is a useful extra layer, but any leaked or shared UUID still opens the ticket without the check.
why: UUIDs make guessing harder, but a leaked link still works without an ownership check.
An encrypted ID is still a token that grants access if it leaks.
Rate limits slow down guessing without stopping it.

quiz.context: This report should list every user, with their open tickets if any. Users who have no open tickets are missing from it.

artifact.code:
SELECT u.email, t.id AS ticket_id
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN tickets t ON t.user_id = u.id
WHERE t.status = 'open';

options: The WHERE on `t.status` drops the NULL rows the left join kept
A left join returns only users who have at least one ticket
The query needs `GROUP BY u.email` to keep every user
The join condition should compare emails instead of IDs
quiz.explain: For users without open tickets, the left join produces a row with NULL ticket columns, then `NULL = 'open'` is UNKNOWN and WHERE drops it. Moving `t.status = 'open'` into the ON clause keeps every user.
why: A left join keeps every left row; that is its purpose.
Grouping cannot bring back rows that WHERE already removed.
Joining on IDs is correct; emails are not the foreign key.

quiz.q: Relay's ticket list joins tickets to users to show each customer's name. A teammate proposes copying the name into every ticket row. What does that trade?
options: Less storage, in exchange for slower writes
Faster reads with no join, in exchange for keeping copies in sync
Stronger consistency, in exchange for more complex queries
Nothing, since Postgres keeps such copies in sync automatically
quiz.explain: Denormalizing removes the join from reads, and every name change must now update all copies or they drift. It uses more storage, not less, and weakens consistency rather than strengthening it.
why: Copies use more storage, not less.
Copies weaken consistency, because they can disagree.
Postgres does not update copies for you unless you build that yourself.

quiz.context: During a 2 p.m. deploy, a migration ran `ALTER TABLE messages ADD COLUMN ...`. For six minutes every request touching messages hung, then everything recovered at once. The same migration took under a second in staging. During the incident, one session had been `idle in transaction` since 1:54 p.m.
quiz.q: What is the most likely explanation?
options: The new column forced a rewrite of the whole messages table
The API ran out of database connections during the deploy
The ALTER waited behind the idle transaction, and new queries queued behind the ALTER
Autovacuum locked the messages table at the same moment
quiz.explain: Adding a column needs a brief exclusive lock, which cannot be granted while another transaction holds any lock on the table. New queries queue behind the waiting ALTER, so the whole table stalls until the old transaction ends. A rewrite is tempting, but it would have been slow in staging too.
why: A rewrite would have been slow in staging too, and would not depend on an idle session.
Connection exhaustion gives connection errors, and would not single out the messages table.
Autovacuum does not take a lock that blocks ordinary reads and writes.

quiz.q: Relay's sign-up code checks that no user has an email before inserting. During a burst of sign-ups, duplicate accounts appeared. What is the reliable fix?
options: Run the check twice before inserting
Keep a cache of known emails in Redis
Add a unique constraint so the database rejects the second insert
Run a nightly job that merges duplicates
quiz.explain: Two concurrent requests can both pass any check made before the insert. A unique constraint is enforced at the moment of the write, so exactly one insert succeeds. A nightly merge cleans up after the damage instead of preventing it.
why: Checking twice narrows the window but two requests can still both pass.
A cache has the same race between reading and writing.
A cleanup job repairs damage after customers have already seen it.

quiz.q: Which of these are real costs of random (version 4) UUID primary keys compared with 64-bit auto-increment integers? Select all that apply.
options: Each key, and every index entry and foreign key holding it, is larger
Inserts land at random places in the primary key index
IDs reveal how many orders the store takes
IDs collide often enough to need retry logic
Sorting by ID no longer follows creation order
quiz.explain: UUIDs are 16 bytes against 8, random values scatter inserts across the index, and their order means nothing. Revealing volume is a weakness of sequential integers, and random UUID collisions are vanishingly rare in practice.

quiz.q: Put the steps of renaming a column with no downtime in order.
items: Deploy code that writes both the old and new columns
Backfill existing rows into the new column in small batches
Deploy code that reads from the new column
Stop writing the old column, then drop it
quiz.explain: At every step, both the running code and the code being rolled out work with the schema as it is. Backfilling before dual writes leaves a gap of rows written in between, and dropping early breaks any reader still running.

quiz.q: Match each constraint to the bug it prevents.
pairs: A ticket saved without a status
Two accounts with the same email
A refund with a negative amount
A message pointing at a ticket that does not exist
Two rows that cannot be told apart
quiz.explain: Each constraint is a small test the database runs on every write. Choosing the right one turns a class of bad data from 'possible and rare' into 'impossible'.

quiz.context: Relay's nightly re-indexing job crashes on messages whose ticket no longer exists. The messages table has a `ticket_id` column but no foreign key. A cleanup script deletes old closed tickets.
quiz.q: Explain how the orphans appeared, how you would find them, and what you would change so it cannot happen again.
rubric: Without a foreign key, nothing stopped the cleanup script deleting tickets that still had messages
Finds orphans with a left join from messages to tickets where the ticket ID is NULL
Decides what to do with existing orphans before adding the constraint
Adds the foreign key with an explicit ON DELETE rule, such as cascade or restrict
Mentions adding it unvalidated then validating, or otherwise avoiding a long lock
quiz.model: The cleanup script deleted tickets, and with no foreign key the database let it leave their messages behind. A left join from messages to tickets where the ticket ID comes back NULL lists them. I would delete or archive those orphans, then add a foreign key on `messages.ticket_id` with an explicit ON DELETE rule: cascade if messages should go with their ticket, restrict if deletion should fail. On a large table I would add it unvalidated and validate it separately to avoid a long lock.

quiz.context: After a prompt change, Relay's `issue_refund` tool started failing on some tickets. Customers get 'something went wrong' instead of a refund.

artifact.code:
ERROR:  insert or update on table "refunds" violates foreign key constraint
        "refunds_order_id_fkey"
DETAIL:  Key (order_id)=(91822) is not present in table "orders".

quiz.q: What is the most likely cause?
options: The orders table is locked by a running migration
The refund amount is larger than the order total
The model passes order IDs that do not exist, and the foreign key blocks them
The database user lacks permission to insert into refunds
quiz.explain: The error says the order ID does not exist in orders, and the failures began with a prompt change, so the model is supplying wrong IDs. The foreign key is doing its job. A lock would cause waiting rather than this error.
why: A lock makes the insert wait or time out; it does not raise a foreign key error.
An amount rule would be a CHECK violation with a different message.
A permission problem raises 'permission denied', not a constraint violation.

drills.title: Refunds doubled overnight
drills.brief: Finance says the 'Refunds issued by Relay' dashboard jumped from about $4,100 a day to almost $9,900 on Tuesday, and asks whether the agent is issuing duplicate refunds. On Monday evening an analyst added a 'refunds by tag' breakdown to the same dashboard. No change to the agent shipped this week.

artifact.title: Refunds dashboard, daily total
artifact.code:
day    refunded
Sat    $4,050
Sun    $3,980
Mon    $4,210
Tue    $9,870
Wed    $9,640

options: Disable the `issue_refund` tool until the agent is fixed
Read a sample of Tuesday's refund conversations
Compare the dashboard with a plain sum over the refunds table for Tuesday
Add a unique constraint on refunds to block duplicates
steps.explain: A plain sum over the source table tells you in one query whether money really moved or only the report changed. Disabling the tool or adding constraints acts on a theory nobody has tested yet.
steps.reveal: A plain sum over refunds for Tuesday is $4,180, in line with the week. Payment records agree. The agent did not refund twice; the dashboard counts some refunds more than once.

steps.q: The table is right and the dashboard is wrong. Where do you look?
options: The refunds table's indexes
The dashboard query, especially anything changed on Monday
The payment provider's API logs
The dashboard tool's cache settings
steps.explain: The number is computed by the query, and the query changed on Monday. Indexes affect speed, not results, and the provider's logs already agree with the table.
steps.reveal: To support the breakdown, the analyst added a join to `ticket_tags` in the base query that the total panel also uses.

artifact.code:
SELECT date(r.created_at) AS day,
       SUM(r.amount_cents)  AS refunded_cents
FROM refunds r
JOIN tickets t      ON t.id = r.ticket_id
JOIN ticket_tags tt ON tt.ticket_id = t.id
GROUP BY day;

steps.q: Why does this query inflate the total?
options: The inner join drops refunds on untagged tickets
GROUP BY on the date merges refunds from different time zones
SUM ignores refunds whose amount is NULL
Each refund appears once per tag on its ticket
steps.explain: A ticket with three tags produces three rows for the same refund, and SUM adds all three. The inner join does drop untagged tickets, which is also wrong, but that lowers the total rather than raising it.
steps.reveal: Tickets with refunds carry about 2.4 tags on average. Untagged tickets vanish from the total, and the rest are counted two to four times.

steps.q: Which fix keeps the tag breakdown and makes the total correct?
options: Compute the total from refunds alone, and build the tag breakdown as a separate query
Change `SUM` to `SUM(DISTINCT r.amount_cents)`
Change both joins to left joins
Divide the total by the average number of tags per ticket
steps.explain: The total and the breakdown have different grains, one row per refund versus one row per refund and tag, so they need different queries. DISTINCT on amounts merges different refunds of equal size, and a left join keeps untagged refunds but still repeats tagged ones.

drills.debrief: Root cause: a one-to-many join to `ticket_tags` was added to a shared query, so each refund was counted once per tag. Duplicate refunds by the agent were the obvious suspect and were ruled out by one query against the source table. The fix gives each panel a query at its own grain. A dashboard test that compares the total with a plain sum over refunds would have caught it on Monday evening. The general lesson: before trusting a total after a join, ask how many matches each row can have.

drills.title: The deploy that froze the API
drills.brief: At 14:02 a deploy started. By 14:03 every Relay endpoint that reads messages was timing out and the load balancer reported 504s. Endpoints that do not touch messages, such as order lookups, are fine. The deploy includes a migration that changes `messages.id` from a 32-bit integer to bigint, because its sequence passed 1.9 billion.

options: Roll the application back to the previous image
Add API pods to absorb the backlog
See what Postgres sessions are waiting on, and on whom
Restart Postgres to clear stuck connections
steps.explain: Only endpoints touching one table are stuck, which points at a lock on that table. Looking at sessions costs seconds and shows the chain. Rolling back the image does not stop a migration already running in the database, and a restart kills every session blindly.
steps.reveal: Hundreds of API queries wait on a lock. So does the migration. One old session is idle inside an open transaction.

artifact.title: pg_stat_activity, abridged
artifact.code:
pid  | state               | wait_event_type | wait_event | xact_start | query
------+---------------------+-----------------+------------+------------+---------------------------
 3117 | idle in transaction | Client          | ClientRead | 13:21:40   | SELECT count(*) FROM mes...
 4502 | active              | Lock            | relation   | 14:02:05   | ALTER TABLE messages ALT...
 4510 | active              | Lock            | relation   | 14:02:06   | SELECT id, role, body FR...
 4511 | active              | Lock            | relation   | 14:02:06   | SELECT id, role, body FR...
(180 more rows like 4510)

steps.q: Which session is the root of the queue?
options: 3117, the transaction left open since 13:21
4502, the migration
4510, the first API query to wait
None of them; Postgres is simply overloaded
steps.explain: The migration needs an exclusive lock and cannot get it while 3117's open transaction holds a lock on the table. The API queries wait behind the migration. 4502 blocks the API directly, but 3117 is what started the chain.
steps.reveal: `pg_blocking_pids(4502)` returns 3117. `pg_blocking_pids(4510)` returns 4502. Session 3117 is an analyst's notebook that ran a count at 13:21 and never committed.

steps.q: API requests have been stuck for two minutes. What do you do right now?
options: Terminate session 3117 so the migration can proceed
Cancel the migration's ALTER TABLE in session 4502
Raise `max_connections` so new requests get through
Restart the API pods
steps.explain: Cancelling the ALTER releases the queue at once, because the notebook's lock does not conflict with ordinary reads and writes. Terminating 3117 is tempting, but it lets the type change start, and that rewrites the whole messages table under an exclusive lock for far longer.
steps.reveal: Within a second of cancelling 4502, the waiting queries complete and the 504s stop. The notebook session is closed after a message to the analyst.

steps.q: How do you make the ID change safely?
options: Rerun the same migration at 3 a.m., when traffic is low
Run the same migration with a longer statement timeout
Expand and contract: a new bigint column, batched backfill, a short switch, and a lock timeout
Drop and recreate the messages table with the new type
steps.explain: The in-place type change rewrites a huge table under an exclusive lock whenever it runs, so a quiet hour only shrinks the audience for the outage. Expand and contract moves the data in small steps, and the lock timeout makes any step that would wait fail fast instead.

drills.debrief: Root cause: a table-rewriting migration queued behind a forgotten open transaction, and every query on messages queued behind the migration. Restarting things was the obvious move and would have cut the 504s only briefly; the chain was visible in `pg_stat_activity` within a minute. Fixes: a `lock_timeout` on every migration, `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` so abandoned transactions end on their own, and expand and contract for type changes. The general lesson: a migration's risk depends on the locks it needs and on what else is holding locks, not on how fast it ran in staging.
